claim: Measures of lung function are heritable.
source: Spirometry measures of pulmonary function have been shown to display significant heritability both in twin designs and genome-wide association studies (GWAS) (Palmer et al., 2001; Ingebrigtsen et al., 2011; Shrine et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies demonstrating heritability of lung function measures.

claim: Reduced pulmonary function is associated with a marked increase in the risk of mortality.
source: Optimal lung (pulmonary) function is vital for the ongoing maintenance of homeostasis, with reduced pulmonary function associated with a marked increase in the risk of mortality (Vasquez et al., 2017; Young et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies showing the association between reduced lung function and mortality risk.

claim: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is one of the leading causes of death worldwide.
source: For instance, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), characterised by an irreversible limitation of airflow, is one of the leading causes of death worldwide (Quaderi and Hurst, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on COPD mortality.

claim: Pulmonary manifestations are common amongst disorders not directly classified as respiratory conditions, including diabetes.
source: Pulmonary manifestations are also common amongst disorders not directly classified as respiratory conditions, including diabetes (Pitocco et al., 2012; Walter et al., 2003), congenital heart disease (Alonso-Gonzalez et al., 2013), and inflammatory bowel disease (Ji et al., 2016; Yilmaz et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies documenting pulmonary manifestations in non-respiratory disorders.

claim: FVC had the largest number of genetic correlations which surpassed Bonferroni correction (N = 35).
source: FVC had the largest number of genetic correlations which surpassed Bonferroni correction (N = 35), followed by FEV1 and FEV1/FVC for which 25 and 8 traits survived multiple testing correction, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of genetic correlation analysis using LDSC.

claim: The trait most significantly correlated with both FEV1 and FVC was waist circumference.
source: The trait most significantly correlated with both FEV1 and FVC was waist circumference – FEV1: rg = −0.19, SE = 0.02, p=5.71×10−20; FVC: rg = −0.24, SE = 0.02, p=9.54×10−33
evidence: The claim is supported by specific genetic correlation statistics from the LDSC analysis.

claim: Asthma demonstrated the most significant correlation with FEV1/FVC (rg = −0.35, SE = 0.05, p=3.49×10−12).
source: whilst asthma demonstrated the most significant correlation with FEV1/FVC (rg = −0.35, SE = 0.05, p=3.49×10−12).
evidence: The claim is supported by specific genetic correlation statistics from the LDSC analysis.

claim: There was evidence of genetic correlation between measures of lung function and circulating levels of both metabolites and hormones.
source: Interestingly, there was evidence of genetic correlation between measures of lung function and circulating levels of both metabolites and hormones.
evidence: The claim is based on the genetic correlation analysis results presented in the study.

claim: Significant genetic correlations were observed with four metabolites (fasting glucose, high-density lipoprotein [HDL], triglycerides, and urate) and two hormones (fasting insulin and leptin) for at least one measure of lung function.
source: Significant genetic correlations were observed with four metabolites (fasting glucose, high-density lipoprotein [HDL], triglycerides, and urate) and two hormones (fasting insulin and leptin) for at least one measure of lung function (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data presented in Table 1 showing genetic correlations.

claim: A 1 mmol/L increase in fasting glucose was associated with a −0.088 (95% confidence interval [CI]: −0.17, −0.01) standard deviation decline in FVC using an inverse variance weighted (IVW) estimator with multiplicative random effects.
source: A 1 mmol/L increase in fasting glucose was associated with a −0.088 (95% confidence interval [CI]: −0.17, −0.01) standard deviation decline in FVC using an inverse variance weighted (IVW) estimator with multiplicative random effects.
evidence: The claim is supported by the Mendelian randomization analysis results.

claim: Elevated fasting glucose was shown to have a negative effect on FEV1: βIVW = −0.096 (95% CI: –0.18, –0.01).
source: Similarly, elevated fasting glucose was also shown to have a negative effect on FEV1: βIVW = −0.096 (95% CI: –0.18, –0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by the Mendelian randomization analysis results.

claim: The MR–Egger intercept was not significantly different from zero in the FEV1 or FVC model, indicating no evidence of unbalanced pleiotropy.
source: Importantly, the MR–Egger intercept was not significantly different from zero in the FEV1 or FVC model, indicating no evidence of unbalanced pleiotropy.
evidence: The claim is based on the MR-Egger regression results testing for pleiotropy.

claim: The conservative genic boundaries only yielded one druggable gene-set enriched with FEV1-associated variants after multiple testing correction (q < 0.05): signalling events mediated by the Hedgehog family.
source: The conservative genic boundaries only yielded one druggable gene-set enriched with FEV1-associated variants after multiple testing correction (q < 0.05): signalling events mediated by the Hedgehog family – β = 0.973, SE = 0.2, p=9.3×10−7, PT <0.5, NGenes = 22 (Supplementary file 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene-set association analysis results.

claim: There were seven and nine unique gene-sets which survived correction for FEV1 and FVC, respectively (q < 0.05) using liberal genic boundaries.
source: Specifically, there were seven and nine unique gene-sets which survived correction for FEV1 and FVC, respectively (q < 0.05, Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene-set association analysis results using liberal boundaries.

claim: The optimum FEV1 genetic score explained approximately 6.4% of the variance in FEV1 measured in the HCS cohort.
source: The optimum FEV1 genetic score explained approximately 6.4% of the variance in FEV1 measured in the HCS cohort, whilst the FVC PGS explained approximately 5.7% of variance in FVC.
evidence: The claim is based on the polygenic score analysis in the independent HCS cohort.

claim: Four of the PES considered had at least a nominally significant association with their respective spirometry measure (p<0.05).
source: Four of the PES considered had at least a nominally significant association with their respective spirometry measure (p<0.05, Table 3, Supplementary file 3b), whilst three survived correction for the number of tests (p<7.14×10−3).
evidence: The claim is supported by the PES association analysis results in the HCS cohort.

claim: Only the class B/2 secretin family receptor FVC PES remained nominally significant after adjustment for genome-wide PGS (β = 0.047, SE = 0.022, p=0.038).
source: We then constructed a model which was adjusted for genome-wide PGS at the same PT as the PES and found that only the class B/2 secretin family receptor FVC PES remained nominally significant (β = 0.047, SE = 0.022, p=0.038, Figure 3c, Supplementary file 3c)
evidence: The claim is supported by the PES association analysis adjusted for genome-wide PGS.

claim: There was a significant depletion of FVC within the 10th percentile (low genetically predicted FVC) of the class B/2 secretin receptor family FVC PES in the HCS cohort, with the odds of being in the lowest decile decreasing by around 20% per standard deviation increase in FVC (OR = 0.80 [95% CI: 0.68, 0.93], p=4.7×10−3).
source: Furthermore, there was a significant depletion of FVC within the 10th percentile (low genetically predicted FVC) of the class B/2 secretin receptor family FVC PES in the HCS cohort, with the odds of being in the lowest decile decreasing by around 20% per standard deviation increase in FVC (OR = 0.80 [95% CI: 0.68, 0.93], p=4.7×10−3).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis of PES percentiles and FVC in the HCS cohort.

claim: 12.17% and 12.05% of the HCS participants in the 90th percentile PGS for FVC and FEV1 respectively had a depleted PES (10th percentile, low predicted lung function by PES).
source: Specifically, 12.17% and 12.05% of the HCS participants in the 90th percentile PGS for FVC and FEV1 respectively had a depleted PES (10th percentile, low predicted lung function by PES).
evidence: The claim is based on the analysis of PGS and PES distributions in the HCS cohort.

claim: A significant association was identified between the FVC PES class B/2 [secretin family receptors] and the expression of WNT3 using a strict FDR threshold q < 0.05 (t = −3.53, p=4.71×10−4, q = 0.028).
source: We identified a significant association between the FVC PES class B/2 [secretin family receptors] and the expression of WNT3 using a strict FDR threshold q < 0.05 (t = −3.53, p=4.71×10−4, q = 0.028)
evidence: The claim is supported by the PES-gene expression correlation analysis in the 1000 genomes cohort.

claim: Using a Bonferroni threshold for the number of genes tested in lung and blood individually, a number of transcriptome-wide significant genes were identified: FEV1: NGenes [Lung]=232, NGenes [Whole blood]=201; FVC: NGenes [Lung]=222, NGenes [Whole blood]=167.
source: Using a Bonferroni threshold for the number of genes tested in lung and blood individually, we identified a number of transcriptome-wide significant genes as follows – FEV1: NGenes [Lung]=232, NGenes [Whole blood]=201; FVC: NGenes [Lung]=222, NGenes [Whole blood]=167 (Supplementary file 3k–n, Figure 4b).
evidence: The claim is supported by the TWAS analysis results.

claim: Four candidate genes were identified satisfying tier one criteria: PPARD, ADORA2B, KCNJ1, and AMT.
source: Four candidate genes were identified satisfying tier one criteria: PPARD, ADORA2B, KCNJ1, and AMT.
evidence: The claim is based on the TWAS results and drug-gene interaction database searches.

claim: Decreased expression of potassium channel gene KCNJ1 was associated with FVC (ZTWAS = −4.60), and this channel can be inhibited by approved compounds such as the antidiabetic drug glimepiride.
source: For instance, decreased expression of potassium channel gene KCNJ1 was associated with FVC (ZTWAS = −4.60), and this channel can be inhibited by approved compounds such as the antidiabetic drug glimepiride.
evidence: The claim is supported by TWAS results and drug-gene interaction data.

claim: Two FEV1-associated genes with tier 1 and/or tier 2 drug interactions, AMT and PYGB, were included in the credible set with a PIP >0.9 or nearing that threshold.
source: Two FEV1-associated genes with tier 1 and/or tier 2 drug interactions, AMT and PYGB, were included in the credible set with a PIP >0.9 or nearing that threshold.
evidence: The claim is supported by the probabilistic finemapping results of TWAS loci.

claim: PYGB (ZTWAS = −6.98, PIP = 0.999, lung SNP weights) encodes a protein involved in glycogenolysis and can be putatively inhibited by the new exploratory treatment for respiratory failure, sivelestat.
source: PYGB (ZTWAS = −6.98, PIP = 0.999, lung SNP weights) encodes a protein involved in glycogenolysis and can be putatively inhibited by the new exploratory treatment for respiratory failure, sivelestat (Figure 4c).
evidence: The claim is supported by TWAS results, finemapping, and drug-gene interaction data.

claim: There were three inhibitors of human proteins with evidence of interaction with a viral protein that also targeted a gene which was a member of a PES candidate gene-set.
source: There were three inhibitors of human proteins with evidence of interaction with a viral protein that also targeted a gene which was a member of a PES candidate gene-set.
evidence: The claim is based on the analysis of host-viral interactomes and PES gene-sets.

claim: Vorinostat (HDAC2 inhibitor) and aminocaproic acid (PLAT inhibitor) both inhibited a SARS-CoV2 'prey protein' and targeted a gene within the pathways in cancer and extracellular matrix (ECM)/ECM-associated proteins PES pathways, respectively.
source: Vorinostat (HDAC2 inhibitor) and aminocaproic acid (PLAT inhibitor) both inhibited a SARS-CoV2 'prey protein' and targeted a gene within the pathways in cancer and extracellular matrix (ECM)/ECM-associated proteins PES pathways, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on the analysis of host-viral interactomes and drug-gene interactions.

claim: Ruxolitinib inhibits the influenza prey protein JAK1, a part of the pathways in cancer gene-set.
source: Similarly, ruxolitinib inhibits the influenza prey protein JAK1, a part of the pathways in cancer gene-set.
evidence: The claim is based on the analysis of host-viral interactomes and drug-gene interactions.

claim: There was an overrepresentation of SARS-CoV2 'prey proteins' amongst four gene-sets related to glucose metabolism, along with insulin and glucagon signalling pathways.
source: Interestingly, there was an overrepresentation of SARS-CoV2 'prey proteins' amongst four gene-sets related to glucose metabolism, along with insulin and glucagon signalling pathways (Table 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by the overrepresentation analysis of SARS-CoV2 prey proteins in glycaemic pathways.

claim: Fourteen SARS-CoV2 'prey proteins' were members of at least one of these gene-sets, with a greater number of interactions amongst these genes than expected by chance (p=4.42×10−12).
source: Fourteen SARS-CoV2 'prey proteins' were members of at least one of these gene-sets, with a greater number of interactions amongst these genes than expected by chance (p=4.42×10−12, Supplementary file 4d).
evidence: The claim is supported by the protein-protein interaction analysis of SARS-CoV2 prey proteins.

claim: 57% of the glycaemic 'prey proteins' had a high-confidence protein–protein interaction with antidiabetic target gene.
source: None of the glycaemic 'prey proteins' were direct target of antidiabetic compounds; however, 57% of these proteins had a high-confidence protein–protein interaction with antidiabetic target gene (Supplementary file 4e–f).
evidence: The claim is based on the protein-protein interaction analysis between SARS-CoV2 prey proteins and antidiabetic drug targets.

claim: GNB1 putatively binds with a SARS-CoV2 non-structural proteins (Nsp7) that forms the part of the replicase/transcriptase complex.
source: For instance, GNB1 putatively binds with a SARS-CoV2 non-structural proteins (Nsp7) that forms the part of the replicase/transcriptase complex, whilst this protein also demonstrated evidence of interacting with 15 proteins modulated by an antidiabetic compound, such as GLP1R, which is the primary target of GLP-1 analogues, including exenatide.
evidence: The claim is based on the host-viral interactome data and protein-protein interaction analysis.

claim: Declines in pulmonary function are overrepresented amongst individuals with diabetes and correlates with poor glycaemic control.
source: These data support previous literature suggesting that declines in pulmonary function are overrepresented amongst individuals with diabetes and correlates with poor glycaemic control (Walter et al., 2003; Davis et al., 2004; Gutiérrez-Carrasquilla et al., 2019; van den Borst et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies on diabetes and lung function.

claim: Acute hyperglycaemia is associated with a significant increase in morbidity and mortality amongst non-diabetic community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) patients.
source: Acute hyperglycaemia is associated with a significant increase in morbidity and mortality amongst non-diabetic community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) patients, which further supports its utility as a treatment target (Lepper et al., 2012; Jensen et al., 2017; Kornum et al., 2007; McAlister et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on hyperglycaemia and pneumonia outcomes.

claim: Even patients with mild hyperglycaemia (serum glucose 6–10.99 mmol/L) have a purported elevated risk of death at 90 days following CAP diagnosis.
source: Notably, even patients with mild hyperglycaemia (serum glucose 6–10.99 mmol/L) have a purported elevated risk of death at 90 days following CAP diagnosis (Lepper et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on mild hyperglycaemia and CAP outcomes.

claim: The association between type 2 diabetes and poor pneumonia outcomes appears to be driven by glycaemic control.
source: whilst the association between type 2 diabetes and poor pneumonia outcomes appears to be driven by glycaemic control (McAlister et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on diabetes, glycaemic control, and pneumonia outcomes.

claim: The intracellular carbohydrate O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine has been recently linked to influenza-associated cytokine storms.
source: Inflammation is likely to be an important component of glycaemic-influenced adverse effects; for instance, the intracellular carbohydrate O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine has been recently linked to influenza-associated cytokine storms (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on O-GlcNAc and influenza.

claim: Magnesium sulfate had enriched targets in the dilated cardiomyopathy PES and has previously shown promise as a repurposing candidate to improve pulmonary function in asthma.
source: For example, magnesium sulfate had enriched targets in the dilated cardiomyopathy PES and has previously shown promise as a repurposing candidate to improve pulmonary function in asthma (Okayama, 1987; Hossein et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by data on drug target enrichment and citations to studies on magnesium sulfate in asthma.

claim: Lung function GWAS summary statistics were obtained from a meta-analysis of the UK Biobank sample with the SpiroMeta consortium cohorts (N = 400,102).
source: We obtained GWAS summary statistics for FEV1, FVC, and their ratio from a meta-analysis of the UK Biobank sample with the SpiroMeta consortium cohorts as outlined extensively elsewhere (N = 400,102) (Shrine et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim describes the source of the GWAS data used in the study.

claim: Phenotypes were adjusted for age, age2, sex, height, smoking status (ever vs. never smoked), and genotyping array before the residuals were subjected to rank inverse-normal transformation.
source: Phenotypes were adjusted for age, age2, sex, height, smoking status (ever vs. never smoked), and genotyping array before the residuals were subjected to rank inverse-normal transformation.
evidence: The claim describes the phenotype adjustment procedure in the lung function GWAS.

claim: The Bonferroni method was utilised for multiple testing correction with the significance threshold set as p<2.9×10−4 (α = 0.05/172).
source: The Bonferroni method was utilised for multiple testing correction with the significance threshold set as p<2.9×10−4 (α = 0.05/172).
evidence: The claim describes the multiple testing correction method used in the genetic correlation analysis.

claim: We selected 32 genome-wide significant variants associated with glucose in approximate linkage equilibrium as IVs (p<5×10−8, r2 < 0.001).
source: We selected 32 genome-wide significant variants associated with glucose in approximate linkage equilibrium as IVs (p<5×10−8, r2 < 0.001) to ensure that variants were both rigorously associated with the exposure and independent from one another.
evidence: The claim describes the instrumental variable selection for Mendelian randomization.

claim: Fasting glucose data for GWAS were obtained from either plasma or whole blood of non-diabetic individuals of European ancestry and corrected to plasma levels (N = 133,310, unit of effect = mmol/L).
source: Fasting glucose data for GWAS were obtained from either plasma or whole blood of non-diabetic individuals of European ancestry and corrected to plasma levels (N = 133,310, unit of effect = mmol/L) (Scott et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim describes the source and characteristics of the fasting glucose GWAS data.

claim: Participants were drawn from the HCS, a population-based cohort of individuals aged between 55 and 85 years, predominantly of European ancestry and residing in Newcastle, New South Wales, Australia.
source: Participants were drawn from the HCS, a population-based cohort of individuals aged between 55 and 85 years, predominantly of European ancestry and residing in Newcastle, New South Wales, Australia.
evidence: The claim describes the characteristics of the Hunter Community Study cohort.

claim: RNAseq normalised read counts (PEER normalised RPKM) were obtained for 23723 genes which survived QC in the Geuvadis dataset.
source: We obtained RNAseq normalised read counts (PEER normalised RPKM) for 23723 genes which survived QC in the Geuvadis dataset (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/arrayexpress/experiments/E-GEUV-1/files/analysis_results/?ref=E-GEUV-1).
evidence: The claim describes the source and characteristics of the gene expression data used.

claim: The Geuvadis project performed RNAseq on transformed LCL for participants in the 1000 genomes project.
source: The Geuvadis project performed RNAseq on transformed LCL for participants in the 1000 genomes project (Lappalainen et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim describes the Geuvadis project and is supported by a citation.

claim: A transcriptome-wide significant gene was defined by accounting for the number of genes with models of genetically regulated expression in lung and whole blood, respectively – lung: p<6.43×10−6(α = 0.05/7776); whole blood: p<8.32×10−6(α = 0.05/6007).
source: A transcriptome-wide significant gene was defined by accounting for the number of genes with models of genetically regulated expression in lung and whole blood, respectively – lung: p<6.43×10−6(α = 0.05/7776); whole blood: p<8.32×10−6(α = 0.05/6007).
evidence: The claim describes the significance threshold used in the TWAS analysis.

claim: The host–SARS-CoV2 interactome was defined using affinity-purification mass spectrometry (NGenes = 332, MiST score ≥0.7, a SAINTexpress BFDR ≤0.05).
source: The host–SARS-CoV2 interactome was defined using affinity-purification mass spectrometry (NGenes = 332, MiST score ≥0.7, a SAINTexpress BFDR ≤0.05) (Gordon et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim describes the source and criteria for the SARS-CoV2 host-viral interactome data.

claim: 91 proteins were selected which both interact with viral proteins expressed by influenza (mass spectrometry) and siRNA-mediated downregulation-reduced viral replication in cultured cells by at least three log10 units while retaining >80% cell viability.
source: We selected 91 proteins which both interact with viral proteins expressed by influenza (mass spectrometry) and siRNA-mediated downregulation-reduced viral replication in cultured cells by at least three log10 units while retaining >80% cell viability (Watanabe et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim describes the criteria for selecting influenza host-viral interaction proteins and is supported by a citation.

claim: The HAdV–host interactome was defined using a protein microarray platform (NGenes = 24), which encompasses 20 viral proteins encoded by five HAdV species.
source: Finally, the HAdV–host interactome was defined using a protein microarray platform (NGenes = 24), which encompasses 20 viral proteins encoded by five HAdV species (Martinez-Martin et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim describes the source and characteristics of the HAdV host-viral interactome data and is supported by a citation.

claim: Pharmacological interventions which seek to control blood glucose may have positive implications both in terms of improving baseline lung function and reducing the risk of adverse consequences after SARS-CoV2 exposure.
source: Pharmacological interventions which seek to control blood glucose may have positive implications both in terms of improving baseline lung function and reducing the risk of adverse consequences after SARS-CoV2 exposure.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the study's findings regarding glucose, lung function, and SARS-CoV2 prey proteins.

claim: Our data strongly supported the efficacy of antihyperglycaemic compounds as repurposing candidates which could act as the impetus for further clinical investigation via randomised controlled trials.
source: Our data strongly supported the efficacy of antihyperglycaemic compounds as repurposing candidates which could act as the impetus for further clinical investigation via randomised controlled trials.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the multiple lines of evidence presented in the study.

claim: There are likely to be opportunities for precision repurposing of existing drugs to enhance lung function and improve patient outcomes.
source: While the development pathway for new compounds is difficult, there are likely to be opportunities for precision repurposing of existing drugs to enhance lung function and improve patient outcomes.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the potential for drug repurposing based on the study's rationale.

claim: Genomics may reveal clinically relevant insights into the biology underlying lung function, and thus, could be leveraged for drug repurposing.
source: Genomics may reveal clinically relevant insights into the biology underlying lung function, and thus, could be leveraged for drug repurposing.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the potential utility of genomics for drug repurposing.

claim: Replicated, well-powered randomised controlled trials, however, are needed to fully resolve the clinical benefit of repurposing antihyperglycaemic compounds to improve lung function and in the context of viral infection.
source: Replicated, well-powered randomised controlled trials, however, are needed to fully resolve the clinical benefit of repurposing antihyperglycaemic compounds to improve lung function and in the context of viral infection.
evidence: The claim acknowledges the need for future clinical trials to validate the findings.

claim: Future work should focus on the relevance of glycaemic biology to specific respiratory illnesses like asthma and COPD.
source: Future work should focus on the relevance of glycaemic biology to specific respiratory illnesses like asthma and COPD.
evidence: The claim is a recommendation for future research directions.

claim: The presence of a viral–prey protein interaction does not necessarily support its essentiality in the viral life cycle, and further data are needed to support this.
source: The presence of a viral–prey protein interaction also does not necessarily support its essentiality in the viral life cycle, and further data are needed to support this.
evidence: The claim is a cautionary statement about the interpretation of viral-prey protein interactions.

claim: It would be interesting to further explore the relationship between the genetic architecture of fasting glucose and expression of these SARS-CoV2 prey proteins.
source: It would also be interesting to further explore the relationship between the genetic architecture of fasting glucose and expression of these SARS-CoV2 prey proteins.
evidence: The claim is a suggestion for future research.

claim: Targeted drug application and repurposing is by its very nature confounded by biological heterogeneity amongst individuals.
source: Targeted drug application and repurposing is by its very nature confounded by biological heterogeneity amongst individuals.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the challenges of drug repurposing based on established knowledge.

claim: Leveraging inter-individual genetic heterogeneity will improve the precision application of novel drug repurposing.
source: We suggest that leveraging inter-individual genetic heterogeneity in this way will improve the precision application of novel drug repurposing.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis about the utility of genetic heterogeneity for precision drug repurposing.

claim: The specific data from this study require future replication and validation in independent cohorts in order to provide greater support to our observed relationships between PES and spirometry measures.
source: The specific data from this study require future replication and validation in independent cohorts in order to provide greater support to our observed relationships between PES and spirometry measures.
evidence: The claim acknowledges the need for replication of the study's findings.

claim: Further study is warranted to dissect the signals encompassed by pathway-specific PGS, particularly in light of what would be observed amongst other pathways without drug targets or in gene-sets associated with other related traits.
source: In addition, further study is warranted to dissect the signals encompassed by pathway-specific PGS, particularly in light of what would be observed amongst other pathways without drug targets or in gene-sets associated with other related traits.
evidence: The claim is a recommendation for future research to better understand pathway-specific PGS.

claim: The clinical implementation in its most basic form would involve common variant genotyping using a commercial SNP array followed by imputation and lung function PES-based stratification of treatment options.
source: The clinical implementation in its most basic form would involve common variant genotyping using a commercial SNP array followed by imputation and lung function PES-based stratification of treatment options.
evidence: The claim describes a proposed clinical implementation strategy for the PES approach.

claim: Our approach to variant and exposure risk stratification can be applied more broadly to identify and implement precision drug repositioning in a range of complex traits.
source: We envisage that our approach to variant and exposure risk stratification can be applied more broadly to identify and implement precision drug repositioning in a range of complex traits.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the broader applicability of the study's approach.

claim: Careful curation of the proposed repurposing candidates will be critical, particularly in the context of pulmonary traits where a variety of currently approved compounds have adverse respiratory effects.
source: Careful curation of the proposed repurposing candidates will therefore be critical, particularly in the context of pulmonary traits where a variety of currently approved compounds have adverse respiratory effects.
evidence: The claim is a cautionary statement about the need for careful evaluation of drug repurposing candidates.

claim: TWAS could be utilised to help overcome issues with determining the direction of suitable pharmacological intervention by identifying druggable genes which are members of candidate PES gene-sets for which a clinically beneficial impact on expression can be predicted.
source: We suggest that TWAS could be utilised to help overcome these issues by identifying druggable genes which are members of candidate PES gene-sets for which a clinically beneficial impact on expression can be predicted.
evidence: The claim is a suggestion for how TWAS can complement the PES approach.

claim: There is evidence of cross-talk between heritable risk at genes associated with lung function and fasting glucose, with the downregulation of the glycogen phosphorylase PYGB (associated with FEV1) observed through the probabilistic finemapping of TWAS loci.
source: Interestingly, we also saw some evidence of cross-talk between heritable risk at genes associated with lung function and fasting glucose, with the downregulation of the glycogen phosphorylase PYGB (associated with FEV1) observed through the probabilistic finemapping of TWAS loci.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the TWAS finemapping results for PYGB.

claim: Genetics-informed approaches will likely be increasingly useful to target novel respiratory interventions and reposition existing compounds.
source: Genetics-informed approaches will likely be increasingly useful to target novel respiratory interventions and reposition existing compounds.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the future utility of genetics-informed approaches.

claim: In future, genetics-based methods could be integrated with other clinical information to further enhance precision drug repurposing.
source: In future, genetics-based methods could be integrated with other clinical information to further enhance precision drug repurposing, whilst further consideration could be given to experimental compounds to enhance the number of repurposing opportunities.
evidence: The claim is a suggestion for future integration of genetics with clinical data.

claim: There are a number of pathophysiological mechanisms postulated to underlie the relationship between glucose and lung function, including fibrosis mediated by hyperglycaemia-accelerated epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and aberrant inflammatory responses to dysglycaemia.
source: There are a number of pathophysiological mechanisms postulated to underlie this relationship, including fibrosis mediated by hyperglycaemia-accelerated epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (Talakatta et al., 2018) and aberrant inflammatory responses to dysglycaemia (Mohanty et al., 2000; Sun et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on mechanisms linking glucose to lung function.

claim: The data extends on previous observational studies to provide novel evidence for a causal relationship between glucose and lung function.
source: Importantly, our data extends on these previous observational studies to provide novel evidence for a causal relationship.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the novelty of the study's causal inference findings.

claim: SARS-CoV2-infected patients with hyperglycaemia are at higher risk of morbidity and mortality.
source: These data support emerging evidence that SARS-CoV2-infected patients with hyperglycaemia are at higher risk of morbidity and mortality (Kumar et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on SARS-CoV2 and hyperglycaemia.

claim: The interaction between PYGB and sivelestat was derived from two public databases curated by DGIdb v.3.0.2, and appropriate caution should be exercised in interpreting this relationship given that PYGB is not the primary target of sivelestat.
source: We acknowledge that the interaction between PYGB and sivelestat was derived from two public databases curated by DGIdb v.3.0.2 (Supplementary file 3w), and appropriate caution should be exercised in interpreting this relationship given that PYGB is not the primary target of sivelestat.
evidence: The claim is a cautionary statement about the interpretation of the PYGB-sivelestat interaction.

claim: There is evidence of a high-confidence biological interaction between PYGB and the gene that encodes the principal target of sivelestat via the STRING database (ELA2, neutrophil elastase).
source: Interestingly, there is evidence of a high-confidence biological interaction between PYGB and the gene that encodes the principal target of sivelestat via the STRING database (ELA2, neutrophil elastase).
evidence: The claim is based on protein-protein interaction data from the STRING database.

claim: An analogous causal estimate was obtained using the weighted median method (FVC: βWeighted median = −0.09 [95% CI: –0.16, –0.04], p=1.87×10−3, FEV1: βWeighted median = −0.07 [95% CI: –0.13, –0.01], p=0.025).
source: Firstly, we obtained an analogous, and statistically significant, causal estimate using the weighted median method (FVC: βWeighted median = −0.09 [95% CI: –0.16, –0.04], p=1.87×10−3, FEV1: βWeighted median = −0.07 [95% CI: –0.13, –0.01], p=0.025).
evidence: The claim is based on the weighted median MR results.

claim: The causal estimate using MR–Egger was in the same direction for FEV1 and FVC; however, it was non-significant (FVC: βMR Egger = –0.13 [95% CI: −0.30, 0.04], p=0.148, FEV1: βMR Egger = –0.12 [95% CI: −0.30, 0.06], p=0.21).
source: An MR–Egger model was then constructed, which includes a non-zero intercept term which can be used as a measure of unbalanced pleiotropy (Bowden et al., 2015). The causal estimate using MR–Egger was in the same direction for FEV1 and FVC; however, it was non-significant (FVC: βMR Egger = –0.13 [95% CI: −0.30, 0.04], p=0.148, FEV1: βMR Egger = –0.12 [95% CI: −0.30, 0.06], p=0.21).
evidence: The claim is based on the MR-Egger regression results.

claim: An analogous causal estimate was derived regardless of which IV was removed in the leave-one-out analysis; however, there were five IVs for which the estimate was marginally non-significant after exclusion (maximum p=0.11, IVW with multiplicative random effects).
source: An analogous causal estimate was derived regardless of which IV was removed; however, there were five IVs (FEV1 model = two outlier single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) , FVC model = four outlier SNPs [two outlier SNPs shared]) for which the estimate was marginally non-significant after exclusion (maximum p=0.11, IVW with multiplicative random effects).
evidence: The claim is based on the leave-one-out sensitivity analysis results.

claim: The five outlier SNPs were annotated to genes with important roles in glycaemic homeostasis and were almost exclusively associated with glycaemic traits or diabetes.
source: We then used a phenome-wide association approach to demonstrate that these five SNPs were (i) annotated to genes with important roles in glycaemic homeostasis and (ii) were almost exclusively associated with glycaemic traits or diabetes (Supplementary file 1g–l).
evidence: The claim is based on the phenome-wide association analysis of the outlier SNPs.

claim: The outlier IVs did not likely represent horizontal pleiotropy, which would bias the causal estimate, but instead were biologically salient IVs with large effects.
source: As a result, we concluded that these IVs did not likely represent horizontal pleiotropy, which would bias the causal estimate, but instead were biologically salient IVs with large effects (Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the phenome-wide association analysis of the outlier SNPs.

claim: There was a significant genetic correlation between the number of cigarettes smoked per day and fasting glucose (rg = 0.16, SE = 0.043), although this was not observed with the 'ever vs. never smoked' phenotype (rg = 0.007, SE = 0.039).

source: The MR IVs for glucose were further checked for association with either 'ever vs. never smoked' and 'cigarettes per day', with none of the IVs demonstrating any association with either smoking phenotype at a genome-wide (p<5×10−8) or suggestive (p<1×10−5) significance threshold (Supplementary file 1m, n).
evidence: The claim is based on the analysis of MR IVs for association with smoking phenotypes.

claim: The posterior mean GCP and IVW estimates were in the same direction and relatively analogous for both spirometry measures to that observed using the larger GWAS covaried for smoking status, with no apparent evidence that the negative relationship between glucose and lung function was influenced by smoking as a collider variable.
source: We leveraged a smaller UK Biobank GWAS of FEV1 and FVC from the Neale Lab that did not adjust for smoking (N = 272,338). The posterior mean GCP and IVW estimates were in the same direction and relatively analogous for both spirometry measures to that observed using the larger GWAS covaried for smoking status, with no apparent evidence that the negative relationship between glucose and lung function was influenced by smoking as a collider variable.
evidence: The claim is based on the analysis using a GWAS not adjusted for smoking to assess collider bias.

claim: These data suggested that there is an effect of fasting glucose on lung function beyond what is directly attributable to a residual impact of smoking.

evidence: The claim is an inference based on the analyses investigating the potential confounding effect of smoking.
